p3c4.essay:
The chapter opens with a seating problem, and I think the seating problem is the chapter. Sonia comes in, Razumihin stands to let her pass, and Raskolnikov starts to wave her to the sofa, remembers that the sofa is his bed, finds that 'too _familiar_', and reshuffles everyone. Then he does the thing that actually costs him something: he introduces her to his mother and sister by her full name and patronymic, 'firmly and insistently', minutes after they have all been discussing Luzhin's phrase about a young woman 'of notorious behaviour'. Nobody says what she is. Everybody knows. Sonia can hardly bear to sit beside two ladies, and what hurts her most, I notice, is not the mother's squint but Dounia's courteous bow, which she finds 'oppressive and painful'. Being treated decently is the one thing she has had no practice at.

What moves me is how little Sonia says and how much one sentence of hers does. She looks round the garret and blurts out, in a whisper, that he gave them everything. Until then the twenty-five roubles were, to his family, a piece of feverish recklessness with money they had scraped together (see [[p3c3]]). Sonia turns the gift into what it also was. Dounia's eyes light up; even the mother softens. Then the two women are out in the street and the mother has her 'presentiment', which Dounia swats down with the facts.

Dostoevsky then cuts three ways, almost like a film. The women walk off. Sonia hurries home with 'a whole new world' opening before her, unaware that a well-dressed stranger who overheard the name Raskolnikov is two yards behind her, and turns out to lodge next door. He is given a full portrait and no name. I would simply keep him in mind.

And Raskolnikov, with Sonia still in the room, turns to Razumihin and asks about Porfiry Petrovitch. The pretext is neat: a ring and his father's watch, pawned with the old woman, which he must reclaim before his mother asks after them. It is also true, which is why it works. He is walking into the investigator's flat of his own accord, and he knows what that looks like: 'The butterfly flies to the light.' The last page is the part I find chilling. All that teasing of Razumihin about pomatum and blushing reads at first like the only lightness these two have shared in the whole book. It is preparation. He needs to be heard laughing as he comes through the door.

annotations.quote: She was wearing a very plain indoor dress, and had on a shabby old-fashioned hat, but she still carried a parasol.
annotations.note: Last night at her father's deathbed ([[p2c7]]) she came in her street finery, parasol and all, though it was dark. Today everything is changed except the parasol. It is the one item that crosses from the working costume to the daughter, and Dostoevsky's 'but she still' makes sure we see it.

annotations.quote: but feeling that the sofa which served him as a bed, was too _familiar_ a place, he hurriedly motioned her to Razumihin’s chair.
annotations.note: A scruple so fine it is almost comic in a man with his secret. He will not seat a girl with her reputation on his bed in front of his mother. The italics are his thought, and they show how exactly he has grasped what Sonia must be feeling.

annotations.quote: “You gave us everything yesterday,” Sonia said suddenly, in reply, in a loud rapid whisper
annotations.note: He asked why she was looking at his room; this is her answer. She has just understood that the benefactor is as poor as they are. It is the first thing she says in the book that is not an errand, and it changes the temperature of the room at once.

annotations.quote: The very streets here feel like shut-up rooms.
annotations.note: The mother, two days in Petersburg, gives the best one-line description of the novel's city. Everything in this book is close, low-ceilinged, airless, and she feels it even outdoors. She has just called her son's room a tomb; now the whole town is one.

annotations.quote: as soon as she came in, that very minute, I felt that she was the chief cause of the trouble
annotations.note: On the facts Dounia is unanswerable: he met the girl two nights ago. But I would not wave the mother away entirely. She is wrong about the cause and right that something in her son turned towards that girl the moment she entered.

annotations.quote: People are happy who have no need of locks
annotations.note: Said laughing, to Sonia, on the stairs. From this man it is a strange joke: the whole of [[p1c7]] turned on doors, a hook, a bolt left undone. And for a night the stolen things sat in this unlocked room, in a hole behind the wallpaper.

annotations.quote: His eyes were blue and had a cold and thoughtful look; his lips were crimson.
annotations.note: A passer-by gets a longer physical description than most of the main cast have had. Fresh colour, spotless gloves, crimson lips: he is too well preserved, and the health itself reads as faintly unwholesome. Dostoevsky does not name him. Notice only that he started at the name Raskolnikov.

annotations.quote: Here this man will go to the stake for me, and I find him delighted at having it _cleared up_ why I spoke of rings in my delirium!
annotations.note: Razumihin's joy gives the game away. If even the most loyal man in Petersburg needed the rings 'cleared up', then the suspicion has been living in everyone's head for days. Raskolnikov learns how far it has spread from the relief of his friend.

annotations.quote: Is it a good thing to go or not? The butterfly flies to the light.
annotations.note: Garnett's butterfly is our moth at the candle. He sees quite clearly that going to the investigator unasked is the moth's move, and he goes. Whether that is cunning or compulsion the sentence leaves open, and so, I think, does he.

annotations.quote: This is what Raskolnikov wanted: from within they could be heard laughing as they came in
annotations.note: The narrator steps in to tell us the Romeo teasing was stagecraft. He has used his friend's first, clumsy love as a prop for his entrance. It is a small act next to the large one, but it is cold in the same way.

links.why: The night before: Sonia in her other dress at her father's deathbed, and the money and the address he handed over.
'The whole history of the dead father floated before his memory' — this is where Marmeladov told it, including what Sonia did for the family.
The scene Sonia has just walked into: the mother's 'tomb', Luzhin's letter, and the talk of watches that sets up his pretext.

p3c5.essay:
This is one of the great conversations in the novel, and almost nothing is said in it outright. Raskolnikov enters laughing, on a cue he has rehearsed; Razumihin smashes a tea-glass; Porfiry Petrovitch, in dressing-gown and trodden-down slippers, answers with a quotation. From then on we are shut inside Raskolnikov's head and never once let into Porfiry's. Did he wink? 'Perhaps it was Raskolnikov's fancy.' That is the method of the whole scene. Every remark has an innocent reading and a deadly one, and we are given exactly as much to go on as the suspect has. 'I have been expecting you here for some time' is said over an ash-tray.

Then comes the surprise the book has been keeping back. We watched the murder through all of Part One believing we knew the motives: poverty, the letter from home, the arithmetic overheard in the tavern in [[p1c6]]. Only now, in the investigator's sitting-room, do we learn that there was a theory, written down six months ago and published. And the author did not know it was in print. Porfiry tells him about his own article. I can't think of a neater way to show who holds the cards.

The theory deserves to be heard fairly, and Raskolnikov states it well. Men divide into the ordinary, who 'live under control and love to be controlled', and the few capable of 'a new word', who have 'not an official right, but an inner right' to 'overstep' obstacles. Garnett's 'overstep' and 'transgress' are worth noticing: the Russian word for crime means literally a stepping-over, so the novel's title is hiding inside the argument. The idea was in the air in 1865, when Napoleon III's book on Julius Caesar had everyone arguing about whether great men answer to ordinary morality, and Raskolnikov himself says there is 'nothing particularly new' in it.

What I notice is how the examples slide. He starts with Newton and Kepler, for whose discoveries nobody had to die, and within a few sentences he is at Lycurgus, Mahomet and Napoleon, 'terrible carnage', and wading through blood. Then the speech ends in numbers: one man in a thousand, one in a hundred thousand, the genius 'one of millions', all produced in a 'retort' by an unknown law. Five minutes earlier Razumihin was shouting that a system 'that has come out of some mathematical brain' leaves out the living soul, and that 'You can't skip over nature by logic.' He thought he was attacking the socialists. He was describing his friend. To his credit he also sees the real point at once, and with horror: what is original here is bloodshed sanctioned 'in the name of conscience', which is worse than any legal licence.

Porfiry never argues. He plays the nervous citizen and asks questions, each one a joke and each one the true objection. Could they wear a uniform? Are there many of them? What if a youth mistakes his category and needs money for his enterprise? To that last Raskolnikov answers, quite calmly, that 'the vain and foolish are particularly apt to fall into that snare; young people especially.' I find that sentence hard to read without wincing. And then his tone gives way altogether. Great men 'must, I think, have great sadness on earth', he says, 'dreamily, not in the tone of the conversation'. For one line the lecturer is gone and someone very tired is speaking.

The strangest turn is the catechism in the middle. Do you believe in the New Jerusalem, in God, in the raising of Lazarus, literally? Raskolnikov has kept his eyes on one spot of carpet throughout and lifts them only at 'God'. Why a magistrate should want to know this the chapter does not say. Hold on to it.

The usual picture of Porfiry is a cat with a mouse, and Raskolnikov uses that very image. I don't quite accept it. 'If only you knew how you interest me!' sounds to me like the truth. He has read the article more attentively than anyone alive, and his interest in the conscience of the man who 'makes a mistake' goes beyond what a conviction needs. The trap at the door, the muddled painters, is real enough, and it is the 'innocent blockhead' Razumihin who catches it. But the trap is the least of what has happened. Someone has finally taken the idea seriously, and it was the police.

annotations.quote: “But why break chairs, gentlemen? You know it’s a loss to the Crown,” Porfiry Petrovitch quoted gaily.
annotations.note: He is quoting Gogol's comedy The Government Inspector, where a schoolmaster gets so carried away describing Alexander the Great that he smashes the furniture: Alexander was a hero, but why break chairs? So Porfiry's first words in the book are a joke about great men as an excuse for damage. Whether he means it that way yet is anyone's guess.

annotations.quote: Raskolnikov could have sworn he winked at him, goodness knows why.
annotations.note: The narrator declines to settle it. 'Perhaps it was Raskolnikov's fancy', then 'there was certainly something of the sort'. We are kept exactly as uncertain as the man on the sofa, which is how the chapter makes a talk about paper and pledges unbearable.

annotations.quote: I have been expecting you here for some time.
annotations.note: Dropped 'as though that was a matter of no importance', while he fusses over Razumihin's cigarette ash. The line could mean only that Raskolnikov's name was on the pledge wrapper. It could mean much more. Porfiry lets the ash-tray do the work of looking away.

annotations.quote: You can’t skip over nature by logic. Logic presupposes three possibilities, but there are millions!
annotations.note: Razumihin is attacking the socialists and their phalanstery, the planned communal building dreamed up by Fourier. But the sentence lands on the man next to him, who reasoned his way to an axe with a sum about one life against a hundred ([[p1c6]]). The best refutation of the theory comes before the theory is stated, from someone who doesn't know he is making it.

annotations.quote: Newton would have had the right, would indeed have been in duty-bound... to _eliminate_ the dozen or the hundred men
annotations.note: Watch the slide inside one sentence from 'right' to 'duty-bound'. And watch the italic verb, a clean administrative word for killing. The example is rigged, too: no one stood between Newton and publication, so the dozen dead cost the argument nothing.

annotations.quote: “And... do you believe in Lazarus’ rising from the dead?”
annotations.note: Of all the miracles, the man four days in the tomb who is called out of it (John 11). Raskolnikov's mother has just said his room is like a tomb ([[p3c3]]). He stammers 'I... I do', and then insists on 'Literally'. I don't know how far to believe him, and I'm not sure he does. Keep this question; the book is not done with it.

annotations.quote: couldn’t they adopt a special uniform, for instance, couldn’t they wear something, be branded in some way?
annotations.note: Porfiry's clowning is the theory's fatal objection. If the extraordinary man is known only by his own inner conviction, then anyone may award himself the title. Raskolnikov calls the remark witty. It is more than that, and he knows it.

annotations.quote: The really great men must, I think, have great sadness on earth
annotations.note: Added 'dreamily, not in the tone of the conversation'. Razumihin asked whether the geniuses ought to suffer, and the answer drifts out of debate into something like confession. It is the most unguarded thing he says to Porfiry, and nobody in the room remarks on it.

annotations.quote: “Oh, come, don’t we all think ourselves Napoleons now in Russia?”
annotations.note: Porfiry is half-quoting Pushkin, whose Eugene Onegin says that we all fancy ourselves Napoleons and count other people as so many zeros. A Russian reader would have heard it at once. It turns Raskolnikov's proud idea into a national cliché, a thing every schoolboy thinks, and that stings more than an accusation.

annotations.quote: with an unpleasant sensation at the very moment he spoke that he need not have said it
annotations.note: The trap is being laid. The painters worked in the second-floor flat only on the day of the murder ([[p1c7]]); his admitted visit was days earlier. To remember them is to place himself on the stairs at the wrong hour. He sees it in time, and overdoes the denial a little with that helpful sofa on the fourth storey.

links.why: The theory in its cheap tavern form: a student's sum about one useless life against a hundred, overheard at exactly the wrong moment.
Why Zametov is sitting in the corner looking embarrassed: the restaurant scene where Raskolnikov taunted him about treasure and how he would have hidden it.
Razumihin's account of Nikolay, Dmitri and the painted flat, which is the material Porfiry builds his 'muddled' question from.
Porfiry asks him to come to the office tomorrow at eleven; this is that appointment.

p3c6.essay:
The chapter falls in three pieces, and each one takes something away from him. In the first he is walking with Razumihin, and for once they speak openly about '_it_'. Raskolnikov explains the trap of the painters with the ease of a specialist: only peasants deny everything; an educated man admits the facts and reinterprets them; 'the more cunning a man is, the simpler the trap he must be caught in.' He hears his own enthusiasm and is startled by it. 'I am getting a relish for certain aspects!' And then, on the very steps of the lodging where his mother is waiting, the analyst vanishes. He runs home in a sweat to grope inside a hole in the wallpaper that he emptied days ago ([[p2c2]]). The distance between the man who can out-think an investigator and the man on his knees feeling in the cracks is the whole of his condition.

Then the artisan. After a chapter of winks and tones, in which nothing Porfiry said could be pinned down, the word comes at last from a stooping stranger in a greasy cap, and it comes plainly: 'Murderer!' Raskolnikov does not deny it. He asks, barely audibly, 'Who is a murderer?' and walks on beside the man for a hundred paces. One oddity I can't account for: Porfiry was 'womanish' in figure, and this man looks 'at a distance remarkably like a woman'. Dostoevsky gives both his accusers the same strange trait within a few pages.

The monologue that follows is the centre of the book so far, and it is easy to mistake for remorse. It is not remorse. Read it against the speech he made an hour ago in [[p3c5]]. There he set out the two categories; here he sorts himself. The real master 'forgets an army in Egypt' and is forgiven, because such people are 'not of flesh but of bronze'. He, on the other hand, crept under an old woman's bed. His objection to his crime is that it is ugly, 'too inartistic', and the name he finds for himself is exact: 'an æsthetic louse'. He does not grieve for the old woman. He will 'never, never forgive' her, and says he would kill her again. What he cannot bear is the discovery that he is the sort of man who suffers over it.

Two things in the speech seem to me worse than anything in the murder chapter. One is the admission, in Garnett's italics, that '_I felt beforehand_' he would say all this afterwards. So the theory was never quite believed, even by its author, and he went ahead. The other is 'I didn't kill a human being, but a principle', followed in the same breath by 'I didn't overstep, I stopped on this side.' That verb again: he committed the crime and still failed to cross. And notice what he told Porfiry, as a joke, about ordinary people who mistake themselves for destroyers: they 'castigate themselves'. He is doing it now, on the sofa, right on schedule.

At the very end of the speech the categories run out. He hates his mother and sister with 'a physical hatred'. He wonders why he hardly ever thinks of Lizaveta, 'as though I hadn't killed her'. And he puts her name next to Sonia's: 'Poor gentle things, with gentle eyes.' The theory has a place for Napoleons and a place for lice. It has none for these two, and they are what his mind reaches for as it goes under.

Then the dream. In the first great dream, [[p1c5]], he was a child trying to stop a killing. Here he repeats his own and it will not take: the axe falls and the old woman laughs, 'noiseless laughter', which is just how Porfiry laughed at him this afternoon. The stairs fill with silent heads. For this man the nightmare is not the gallows. It is being laughed at, and watched.

The seam between dream and waking is beautifully made. A fly strikes the pane in the dream; a fly is buzzing at the real window; a stranger sits by the sofa with his chin on his cane. The fair beard and the cane are ones we have seen before, at Sonia's heels in [[p3c4]]. And the name he gives has hung over the family since the mother's letter in [[p1c3]].

annotations.quote: Because only peasants, or the most inexperienced novices deny everything flatly at examinations.
annotations.note: The former law student, lecturing his friend on how a guilty man ought to answer. Razumihin hears a clever, insulted innocent. We hear someone who has thought it all through from the inside, and who is beginning to enjoy explaining it.

annotations.quote: Then in senseless terror he rushed to the corner, to that hole under the paper where he had put the things
annotations.note: The hole has been empty since he carried everything out and buried it under a stone ([[p2c2]]). A minute ago he was saying that clever people are caught by stupid things. Here he is, searching every 'crack and fold' for the stupid thing.

annotations.quote: wearing a long coat and a waistcoat, and looking at a distance remarkably like a woman
annotations.note: An odd detail to give a man about to speak the heaviest word in the book. Porfiry too was described as 'womanish', twice. I have no confident reading of this; I only notice that both accusers are made soft, stooped and unthreatening to look at.

annotations.quote: “Murderer!” he said suddenly in a quiet but clear and distinct voice.
annotations.note: Nobody has said this to him before. Porfiry circled it with jokes about Napoleons; this man simply says it, quietly, in the street, and walks on. The effect is physical: weak legs, a shiver, a heart that stops and then throbs 'as though it were set free'. Set free is a curious phrase for terror.

annotations.quote: No, such people, it seems, are not of flesh but of bronze!
annotations.note: The list before it is Napoleon's career as a rap sheet: Toulon, the cannon fired on a Paris crowd, the army abandoned in Egypt, the retreat from Moscow shrugged off with a quip. Garnett's italics on '_forgets_' and '_wastes_' carry his envy. He admires the lack of feeling most of all, and it is the one thing he has just found he hasn't got.

annotations.quote: Ech, I am an æsthetic louse and nothing more
annotations.note: 'Louse' was the word for the old woman in the tavern talk of [[p1c6]]; now he pins it on himself. 'Æsthetic' is the cruel half. He wanted his crime to be handsome, and his complaint about it is a complaint of taste.

annotations.quote: It’s for you to obey, trembling creation, and not _to have desires_, for that’s not for you!
annotations.note: The phrase comes from Pushkin's poems imitating the Koran, where the Prophet's God addresses the 'trembling creature'. Raskolnikov has fused Mahomet with Napoleon's street battery into one figure who never explains himself. Note which side of the sentence he is now standing on.

annotations.quote: It’s strange though, why is it I scarcely ever think of her, as though I hadn’t killed her?
annotations.note: Lizaveta, the second victim, the one no theory required. He has raged about the old woman for pages and this is nearly the first thought he has spared the sister. I think the silence is the measure of it: the pawnbroker he can argue with, Lizaveta he cannot.

annotations.quote: the old woman was sitting and laughing, shaking with noiseless laughter, doing her utmost that he should not hear it
annotations.note: Porfiry 'laughed noiselessly' when he asked whether Raskolnikov could rob and murder ([[p3c5]]). The dream hands that laugh to the victim. He kills her again and she finds it funny, and then the laughter spreads to the next room and the stairs.

annotations.quote: Only a big fly buzzed and fluttered against the window pane.
annotations.note: The fly was in the dream a moment ago, striking the moonlit pane, and before that in his waking thoughts: 'A fly flew by and saw it!' Now it is in the room. Dostoevsky stitches nightmare to daylight with one insect, so that the man in the chair seems to have walked out of the dream.

links.why: The first great dream, of the beaten mare; set the child who tried to stop that killing beside the man who repeats this one.
The real staircase, flat and axe that the dream restages, down to the bedroom door and the people on the stairs.
The theory as he delivered it to Porfiry an hour earlier; the monologue here is the same speech turned on himself.
The stranger in the doorway has only given his name; here he starts to talk.
